title: Connect Database
summary: DB = automation memory — a single place with fixed fields for writing and reading.

sections.heading: Orientation — Lesson Start
sections.subtitle: Lesson Start
sections.contentMarkdown:
- **What will you understand?** Automation becomes more powerful when it stores organized data — not just sends a message and forgets.
- **Why now?** The **workflow** reads and writes — without a clear place for data, repetitive tasks revert to manual work.
- **What after the lesson?** You will choose where the **workflow** stores the data and what fields it needs.

sections.heading: Tension — A Familiar Situation
sections.subtitle: A Familiar Situation
sections.contentMarkdown:
- "The customer registered — but we can't find their data."
- Automation sends a welcome email — good. But when sales asks, "Who is this customer?" — there is no record.
- The data went into the email only — not in an organized place to refer to every day.
- The default worker needs memory: Where to store? What fields? When to read? — without that, repetitive tasks revert to manual work.

sections.heading: Core Idea — DB = Automation Memory
sections.subtitle: DB = Automation Memory
sections.contentMarkdown:
- Every lead or request needs to be recorded in one place — a table or organized sheet with fixed fields.
- Write: When is the data written? (after registration) — When is it read? (daily report, follow-up).
- Three fields are enough to start: Name, Contact, Date/Status — you don't need 20 columns.
- The **workflow** reads from the same place it writes — that’s what makes repetitive tasks work automatically.

sections.heading: Comparison — Email Only vs Organized Record
sections.subtitle: Email Only vs Organized Record
sections.contentMarkdown:
| Email Only | Record + Email |
|----------|------------|
| Automation sends an email — the data is in the inbox. After a week: Who registered? No one knows. | The same automation writes a row in a table (Name, Phone, Date) + sends an email. Follow-up is automatic. |

sections.heading: Glossary — Two Terms for Storage
sections.subtitle: Two Terms for Storage
sections.contentMarkdown:
| Term | Meaning | Example |

| **Schema** | The fields you store — the name and type of each column | leads: name, phone, status, created_at |
| **CRUD** | Create = Write. Read = Read. Update = Update. Delete = Delete | New registration → Create. Daily report → Read |

sections.heading: Screenshot Block (Intent)
sections.contentMarkdown: Every event (registration, progress, request) is recorded in one place. The **workflow** reads and writes from the same source — not scattered files.

sections.heading: Quiz — Quick Confirmation
sections.subtitle: Quick Confirmation
sections.contentMarkdown:
**Question:** Automation registers new customers every day. Sales needs a report with their names. What is most important?

- **Correct Answer:** **The workflow writes each customer in an organized table with fixed fields — and reads from it for the report.**
- **Explanation:** The organized record = automation memory. Email without a table = repetitive tasks revert to manual work.

sections.heading: Mission — Define Where to Store Data
sections.subtitle: Define Where to Store Data
sections.contentMarkdown:
**Introduction:** The mission is design — not a mandatory technical connection. Choose a **workflow** and define: Where will the data be stored? What fields? AI can suggest columns — you choose the final ones.

**Delivery:** **Workflow** · Storage location · At least 3 fields · When to write (after which **trigger**) · When to read (who uses it and why)

**Evaluation Criteria:**

| Dimension | Weight | Criteria |
|-------|-------|---------|
| Location + Fields | 60% | A defined storage location — not "we'll see"; at least 3 fields with clear names |
| Writing and Reading | 40% | When to write linked to the **trigger**; when to read with a clear user |
